stem: A current of 0.5 A is drawn by a filament of an electric bulb for 10 minutes. Find the amount of electric charge that flows through the circuit.
solution:
We are given, \(I = 0.5\,\text{A}\); \(t = 10\,\text{min} = 600\,\text{s}\).

From Eq. (11.1), we have

\(Q = It\)

\(= 0.5\,\text{A} \times 600\,\text{s}\)

\(= 300\,\text{C}\)

stem: How much work is done in moving a charge of 2 C across two points having a potential difference 12 V?
solution:
The amount of charge \(Q\), that flows between two points at potential difference \(V\) (= 12 V) is 2 C. Thus, the amount of work \(W\), done in moving the charge [from Eq. (11.2)] is

\(W = VQ\)

\(= 12\,\text{V} \times 2\,\text{C}\)

\(= 24\,\text{J}\)

stem: (a) How much current will an electric bulb draw from a 220 V source, if the resistance of the bulb filament is 1200 \(\Omega\)? (b) How much current will an electric heater coil draw from a 220 V source, if the resistance of the heater coil is 100 \(\Omega\)?
solution:
(a) We are given \(V = 220\,\text{V}\); \(R = 1200\,\Omega\).

From Eq. (11.6), we have the current \(I = 220\,\text{V} / 1200\,\Omega = 0.18\,\text{A}\).

(b) We are given, \(V = 220\,\text{V}\), \(R = 100\,\Omega\).

From Eq. (11.6), we have the current \(I = 220\,\text{V} / 100\,\Omega = 2.2\,\text{A}\).

Note the difference of current drawn by an electric bulb and electric heater from the same 220 V source!

stem: The potential difference between the terminals of an electric heater is 60 V when it draws a current of 4 A from the source. What current will the heater draw if the potential difference is increased to 120 V?
solution:
We are given, potential difference \(V = 60\,\text{V}\), current \(I = 4\,\text{A}\).

According to Ohm's law, \(R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{60\,\text{V}}{4\,\text{A}} = 15\,\Omega\).

When the potential difference is increased to 120 V the current is given by

\(\text{current} = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{120\,\text{V}}{15\,\Omega} = 8\,\text{A}\).

The current through the heater becomes 8 A.
groundedIn: §11.4 Ohm's law — the resistance stays the same, so the current rises in proportion to \(V\).

stem: Resistance of a metal wire of length 1 m is 26 \(\Omega\) at 20°C. If the diameter of the wire is 0.3 mm, what will be the resistivity of the metal at that temperature? Using Table 11.2, predict the material of the wire.
solution:
We are given the resistance \(R\) of the wire \(= 26\,\Omega\), the diameter \(d = 0.3\,\text{mm} = 3 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}\), and the length \(l\) of the wire \(= 1\,\text{m}\).

Therefore, from Eq. (11.10), the resistivity of the given metallic wire is

\(\rho = (RA/l) = (R\pi d^2 / 4l)\)

Substitution of values in this gives

\(\rho = 1.84 \times 10^{-6}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\)

The resistivity of the metal at 20°C is \(1.84 \times 10^{-6}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\). From Table 11.2, we see that this is the resistivity of manganese.
groundedIn: §11.5, Eq. (11.10) \(R = \rho l / A\), and Table 11.2 for the material.

stem: A wire of given material having length \(l\) and area of cross-section \(A\) has a resistance of 4 \(\Omega\). What would be the resistance of another wire of the same material having length \(l/2\) and area of cross-section \(2A\)?
solution:
For first wire

\(R_1 = \rho \dfrac{l}{A} = 4\,\Omega\)

Now for second wire

\(R_2 = \rho \dfrac{l/2}{2A} = \dfrac{1}{4}\,\rho\,\dfrac{l}{A}\)

\(R_2 = \dfrac{1}{4} R_1\)

\(R_2 = 1\,\Omega\)

The resistance of the new wire is \(1\,\Omega\).
groundedIn: §11.5, Eq. (11.10) — resistance varies directly with length and inversely with area of cross-section.

stem: An electric lamp, whose resistance is 20 \(\Omega\), and a conductor of 4 \(\Omega\) resistance are connected to a 6 V battery (Fig. 11.9). Calculate (a) the total resistance of the circuit, (b) the current through the circuit, and (c) the potential difference across the electric lamp and conductor.
solution:
The resistance of electric lamp, \(R_1 = 20\,\Omega\),

The resistance of the conductor connected in series, \(R_2 = 4\,\Omega\).

Then the total resistance in the circuit

\(R_s = R_1 + R_2 = 20\,\Omega + 4\,\Omega = 24\,\Omega\).

The total potential difference across the two terminals of the battery \(V = 6\,\text{V}\).

Now by Ohm's law, the current through the circuit is given by

\(I = V/R_s = 6\,\text{V} / 24\,\Omega = 0.25\,\text{A}\).

Applying Ohm's law to the electric lamp and conductor separately, we get potential difference across the electric lamp,

\(V_1 = 20\,\Omega \times 0.25\,\text{A} = 5\,\text{V}\);

and that across the conductor,

\(V_2 = 4\,\Omega \times 0.25\,\text{A} = 1\,\text{V}\).

stem: In the circuit diagram given in Fig. 11.10, suppose the resistors \(R_1\), \(R_2\) and \(R_3\) have the values 5 \(\Omega\), 10 \(\Omega\), 30 \(\Omega\), respectively, which have been connected to a battery of 12 V. Calculate (a) the current through each resistor, (b) the total current in the circuit, and (c) the total circuit resistance.
solution:
\(R_1 = 5\,\Omega\), \(R_2 = 10\,\Omega\), and \(R_3 = 30\,\Omega\).

Potential difference across the battery, \(V = 12\,\text{V}\). This is also the potential difference across each of the individual resistor; therefore, to calculate the current in the resistors, we use Ohm's law.

The current \(I_1\), through \(R_1 = V/R_1 = 12\,\text{V}/5\,\Omega = 2.4\,\text{A}\).

The current \(I_2\), through \(R_2 = V/R_2 = 12\,\text{V}/10\,\Omega = 1.2\,\text{A}\).

The current \(I_3\), through \(R_3 = V/R_3 = 12\,\text{V}/30\,\Omega = 0.4\,\text{A}\).

The total current in the circuit,

\(I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3 = (2.4 + 1.2 + 0.4)\,\text{A} = 4\,\text{A}\)

The total resistance \(R_p\), is given by [Eq. (11.18)]

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{1}{3}\)

Thus, \(R_p = 3\,\Omega\).

stem: If in Fig. 11.12, \(R_1 = 10\,\Omega\), \(R_2 = 40\,\Omega\), \(R_3 = 30\,\Omega\), \(R_4 = 20\,\Omega\), \(R_5 = 60\,\Omega\), and a 12 V battery is connected to the arrangement. Calculate (a) the total resistance in the circuit, and (b) the total current flowing in the circuit.
solution:
Suppose we replace the parallel resistors \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) by an equivalent resistor of resistance, \(R'\). Similarly we replace the parallel resistors \(R_3\), \(R_4\) and \(R_5\) by an equivalent single resistor of resistance \(R''\). Then using Eq. (11.18), we have

\(1/R' = 1/10 + 1/40 = 5/40\); that is \(R' = 8\,\Omega\).

Similarly, \(1/R'' = 1/30 + 1/20 + 1/60 = 6/60\); that is, \(R'' = 10\,\Omega\).

Thus, the total resistance, \(R = R' + R'' = 18\,\Omega\).

To calculate the current, we use Ohm's law, and get

\(I = V/R = 12\,\text{V}/18\,\Omega = 0.67\,\text{A}\).
groundedIn: §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18), with the series rule of §11.6.1 applied to the two equivalent resistors; Fig. 11.12.

stem: An electric iron consumes energy at a rate of 840 W when heating is at the maximum rate and 360 W when the heating is at the minimum. The voltage is 220 V. What are the current and the resistance in each case?
solution:
From Eq. (11.19), we know that the power input is

\(P = VI\)

Thus the current \(I = P/V\)

(a) When heating is at the maximum rate,

\(I = 840\,\text{W} / 220\,\text{V} = 3.82\,\text{A}\);

and the resistance of the electric iron is

\(R = V/I = 220\,\text{V} / 3.82\,\text{A} = 57.60\,\Omega\).

(b) When heating is at the minimum rate,

\(I = 360\,\text{W} / 220\,\text{V} = 1.64\,\text{A}\);

and the resistance of the electric iron is

\(R = V/I = 220\,\text{V} / 1.64\,\text{A} = 134.15\,\Omega\).
groundedIn: §11.7, Eq. (11.19) \(P = VI\), with Ohm's law from §11.4.

stem: 100 J of heat is produced each second in a 4 \(\Omega\) resistance. Find the potential difference across the resistor.
solution:
\(H = 100\,\text{J}\), \(R = 4\,\Omega\), \(t = 1\,\text{s}\), \(V = ?\)

From Eq. (11.21) we have the current through the resistor as

\(I = \sqrt{H/Rt}\)

\(= \sqrt{100\,\text{J} / (4\,\Omega \times 1\,\text{s})}\)

\(= 5\,\text{A}\)

Thus the potential difference across the resistor, \(V\) [from Eq. (11.5)] is

\(V = IR\)

\(= 5\,\text{A} \times 4\,\Omega\)

\(= 20\,\text{V}\).
groundedIn: §11.7, Eq. (11.21) \(H = I^2 Rt\) (Joule's law of heating), with Ohm's law.

stem: An electric bulb is connected to a 220 V generator. The current is 0.50 A. What is the power of the bulb?
An electric refrigerator rated 400 W operates 8 hour/day. What is the cost of the energy to operate it for 30 days at Rs 3.00 per kW h?
solution:
The total energy consumed by the refrigerator in 30 days would be

\(400\,\text{W} \times 8.0\,\text{hour/day} \times 30\,\text{days} = 96000\,\text{W h}\)

\(= 96\,\text{kW h}\)

Thus the cost of energy to operate the refrigerator for 30 days is

\(96\,\text{kW h} \times \text{Rs } 3.00 \text{ per kW h} = \text{Rs } 288.00\)
groundedIn: §11.8, where the kilowatt hour is defined as the commercial unit of electric energy.

stem: What does an electric circuit mean?
solution:
An electric circuit is a continuous, closed path along which an electric current can flow.

It is made up of a cell or battery (the source of potential difference), connecting wires, a plug key or switch, and one or more electrical components such as a bulb, a resistor or an ammeter. When the key is closed the path is unbroken and current flows; when the key is open the path is broken and the current stops.
groundedIn: §11.1 and Fig. 11.1, the schematic circuit of a cell, bulb, ammeter and plug key.

stem: Define the unit of current.
solution:
The SI unit of electric current is the **ampere (A)**, named after the French scientist Andre-Marie Ampere.

One ampere is the current constituted by the flow of one coulomb of charge per second, that is

\(1\,\text{A} = 1\,\text{C} / 1\,\text{s}\)
groundedIn: §11.1 — 'One ampere is constituted by the flow of one coulomb of charge per second.'

stem: Calculate the number of electrons constituting one coulomb of charge.
solution:
One electron carries a charge of \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\).

Number of electrons in one coulomb

\(n = \dfrac{1\,\text{C}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}} = 6.25 \times 10^{18}\)

So about \(6 \times 10^{18}\) electrons make up one coulomb of charge.
groundedIn: §11.1 — one coulomb is 'the charge contained in nearly \(6 \times 10^{18}\) electrons', each of charge \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C.

stem: Name a device that helps to maintain a potential difference across a conductor.
solution:
A **cell**, or a **battery** made of several cells, maintains a potential difference across a conductor.

The chemical action within a cell generates a potential difference across its terminals even when no current is drawn from it, and the cell expends its stored chemical energy to keep that difference up while current flows.
groundedIn: §11.2 — 'This difference of potential may be produced by a battery, consisting of one or more electric cells.'

stem: What is meant by saying that the potential difference between two points is 1 V?
solution:
Saying that the potential difference between two points is 1 V means that **1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb from one point to the other**.

\(1\,\text{V} = \dfrac{1\,\text{joule}}{1\,\text{coulomb}} = 1\,\text{J}\,\text{C}^{-1}\)
groundedIn: §11.2, Eq. (11.3) — the definition of the volt.

stem: How much energy is given to each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery?
solution:
From \(V = W/Q\), the energy given to a charge \(Q\) is \(W = VQ\).

\(W = 6\,\text{V} \times 1\,\text{C} = 6\,\text{J}\)

So each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery is given 6 joules of energy.

stem: On what factors does the resistance of a conductor depend?
groundedIn: §11.5, Eq. (11.10) — the resistance depends directly on length, inversely on area of cross-section, and on the material; temperature dependence is stated alongside Table 11.2.

stem: Will current flow more easily through a thick wire or a thin wire of the same material, when connected to the same source? Why?
solution:
Current flows more easily through the **thick wire**.

Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section, \(R = \rho l / A\). A thick wire has a larger area of cross-section, so its resistance is smaller. For the same potential difference, \(I = V/R\) is then larger, so a thick wire carries more current than a thin one of the same material and length.
groundedIn: §11.5, Eq. (11.10), with Ohm's law from §11.4.

stem: Let the resistance of an electrical component remains constant while the potential difference across the two ends of the component decreases to half of its former value. What change will occur in the current through it?
solution:
By Ohm's law \(I = V/R\). With \(R\) constant, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference.

If \(V\) falls to \(V/2\), the new current is

\(I' = \dfrac{V/2}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{I}{2}\)

So the current also **falls to half** its former value.
groundedIn: §11.4 Ohm's law — the current is directly proportional to the potential difference at constant temperature.

stem: Why are coils of electric toasters and electric irons made of an alloy rather than a pure metal?
solution:
Two reasons, both of which matter for a heating device:

- **The resistivity of an alloy is generally much higher than that of its constituent metals**, so an alloy coil has a high resistance and produces far more heat for the same current \(\left(H = I^2 Rt\right)\).
- **Alloys do not oxidise, or burn, readily at high temperatures**, so the coil survives being run red-hot again and again.
groundedIn: §11.5 — 'the resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals. Alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures. For this reason, they are commonly used in electrical heating devices'; see also Table 11.2.

context: Use the data in Table 11.2 to answer the following –
stem: Which among iron and mercury is a better conductor?
solution:
**Iron** is the better conductor.

From Table 11.2, the resistivity of iron is \(10.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\) while that of mercury is \(94.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\). The lower the resistivity, the better the conductor, and iron's resistivity is almost ten times smaller.
groundedIn: Table 11.2 — electrical resistivity of some substances at 20°C.

context: Use the data in Table 11.2 to answer the following –
stem: Which material is the best conductor?
solution:
**Silver** is the best conductor.

Its resistivity, \(1.60 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\), is the lowest of every material listed in Table 11.2 — just below copper at \(1.62 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\).
groundedIn: Table 11.2 — electrical resistivity of some substances at 20°C.

stem: Draw a schematic diagram of a circuit consisting of a battery of three cells of 2 V each, a 5 \(\Omega\) resistor, an 8 \(\Omega\) resistor, and a 12 \(\Omega\) resistor, and a plug key, all connected in series.
solution:
Draw a single closed loop, and place around it, in order: the battery, the plug key and the three resistors.

- The **battery** is three cells joined end to end, each drawn as a long line (positive) beside a short thick line (negative), giving a total of \(3 \times 2\,\text{V} = 6\,\text{V}\).
- The **plug key** is drawn as \(-(\bullet)-\) for a closed key.
- The three **resistors**, 5 \(\Omega\), 8 \(\Omega\) and 12 \(\Omega\), are drawn as zig-zag symbols one after another along the loop, so the same current passes through each in turn.

Because they are in series the total resistance is \(5 + 8 + 12 = 25\,\Omega\).

Use the symbols of Table 11.1 and the layout of Fig. 11.6 as the model.
groundedIn: Table 11.1 for the component symbols and Fig. 11.6 for the series layout; §11.6.1 for the series rule.

stem: Redraw the circuit of Question 1, putting in an ammeter to measure the current through the resistors and a voltmeter to measure the potential difference across the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor. What would be the readings in the ammeter and the voltmeter?
solution:
The **ammeter** goes in series, anywhere in the loop, because the same current flows throughout a series circuit. The **voltmeter** goes in parallel, connected across the two ends of the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor alone.

Total resistance \(R_s = 5\,\Omega + 8\,\Omega + 12\,\Omega = 25\,\Omega\).

Total potential difference \(V = 3 \times 2\,\text{V} = 6\,\text{V}\).

Ammeter reading:

\(I = \dfrac{V}{R_s} = \dfrac{6\,\text{V}}{25\,\Omega} = 0.24\,\text{A}\)

Voltmeter reading, across the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor:

\(V_{12} = IR = 0.24\,\text{A} \times 12\,\Omega = 2.88\,\text{V} \approx 2.9\,\text{V}\)
groundedIn: §11.1 (an ammeter is always connected in series) and §11.2 (a voltmeter is always connected in parallel); the arithmetic uses Eq. (11.14) and Ohm's law.

context: Judge the equivalent resistance when the following are connected in parallel –
stem: 1 \(\Omega\) and \(10^6\,\Omega\)
solution:
\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{10^6} = 1.000001\)

\(R_p \approx 0.999999\,\Omega\), which is **just under 1 \(\Omega\)**.

The point to notice: in a parallel combination the equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest resistance present, and a very large resistance in parallel makes almost no difference at all.
groundedIn: §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18) — the reciprocal of the equivalent resistance is the sum of the reciprocals.

context: Judge the equivalent resistance when the following are connected in parallel –
stem: 1 \(\Omega\) and \(10^3\,\Omega\), and \(10^6\,\Omega\)
solution:
\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{10^3} + \dfrac{1}{10^6} = 1.001001\)

\(R_p \approx 0.999\,\Omega\), again **slightly less than 1 \(\Omega\)**.

The equivalent resistance is dominated by the smallest resistor in the group; the two large ones barely contribute.

stem: An electric lamp of 100 \(\Omega\), a toaster of resistance 50 \(\Omega\), and a water filter of resistance 500 \(\Omega\) are connected in parallel to a 220 V source. What is the resistance of an electric iron connected to the same source that takes as much current as all three appliances, and what is the current through it?
solution:
First find the equivalent resistance of the three appliances in parallel:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{100} + \dfrac{1}{50} + \dfrac{1}{500} = \dfrac{5 + 10 + 1}{500} = \dfrac{16}{500}\)

\(R_p = \dfrac{500}{16} = 31.25\,\Omega\)

The electric iron is to draw the same total current from the same source, so it must have the same resistance:

\(R = 31.25\,\Omega\)

The current through it is

\(I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{220\,\text{V}}{31.25\,\Omega} = 7.04\,\text{A}\)
groundedIn: §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18), with Ohm's law from §11.4.

stem: What are the advantages of connecting electrical devices in parallel with the battery instead of connecting them in series?
solution:
- **Each device gets the full voltage of the source.** In series the potential difference is shared out, so every device runs below its rating.
- **Each device draws the current it needs.** A series circuit forces the same current through everything, which is impracticable when, say, a bulb and a heater need very different currents.
- **One device failing does not stop the others.** In series, a single broken component breaks the whole circuit and nothing works — which is why a single dead bulb puts out a whole string of fairy lights.
- **The total resistance of the circuit is reduced**, so a larger total current can be drawn.
- Each device can be **switched on and off independently**.
groundedIn: §11.6.2 — the discussion following Example 11.9 on why series circuits are impracticable and how a parallel circuit divides the current.

context: How can three resistors of resistances 2 \(\Omega\), 3 \(\Omega\), and 6 \(\Omega\) be connected to give a total resistance of
stem: 4 \(\Omega\)?
solution:
Connect the **3 \(\Omega\) and 6 \(\Omega\) in parallel**, and put the **2 \(\Omega\) in series** with that combination.

Parallel part:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{2 + 1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(R_p = 2\,\Omega\)

Total:

\(R = 2\,\Omega + 2\,\Omega = 4\,\Omega\)
groundedIn: §11.6.1 for the series rule Eq. (11.14) and §11.6.2 for the parallel rule Eq. (11.18).

context: How can three resistors of resistances 2 \(\Omega\), 3 \(\Omega\), and 6 \(\Omega\) be connected to give a total resistance of
stem: 1 \(\Omega\)?
solution:
Connect **all three in parallel**.

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{3 + 2 + 1}{6} = 1\)

\(R_p = 1\,\Omega\)

context: What is (a) the highest, (b) the lowest total resistance that can be secured by combinations of four coils of resistance 4 \(\Omega\), 8 \(\Omega\), 12 \(\Omega\), 24 \(\Omega\)?
stem: The highest total resistance
solution:
The highest total resistance is obtained by connecting **all four coils in series**, because a series combination is greater than any individual resistance:

\(R_s = 4 + 8 + 12 + 24 = 48\,\Omega\)
groundedIn: §11.6.1, Eq. (11.14) — the series combination 'is thus greater than any individual resistance'.

context: What is (a) the highest, (b) the lowest total resistance that can be secured by combinations of four coils of resistance 4 \(\Omega\), 8 \(\Omega\), 12 \(\Omega\), 24 \(\Omega\)?
stem: The lowest total resistance
solution:
The lowest total resistance is obtained by connecting **all four coils in parallel**:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{24} = \dfrac{6 + 3 + 2 + 1}{24} = \dfrac{12}{24} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(R_p = 2\,\Omega\)
groundedIn: §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18) — a parallel combination is smaller than the smallest individual resistance.

stem: Why does the cord of an electric heater not glow while the heating element does?
solution:
The cord and the heating element carry the **same current**, because they are in series. By Joule's law \(H = I^2 Rt\), the heat produced then depends on the resistance.

The heating element is made of an alloy of **high resistivity** and is long and thin, so its resistance is large and a great deal of heat is produced in it — enough to make it glow. The cord is made of copper, whose resistivity is very low, and it is thick, so its resistance is very small and hardly any heat is produced in it. Its temperature stays low and it does not glow.
groundedIn: §11.7, Eq. (11.21) \(H = I^2 Rt\), with the resistivity figures of Table 11.2 and the remarks on alloys in §11.5.

stem: Compute the heat generated while transferring 96000 coulomb of charge in one hour through a potential difference of 50 V.
solution:
The work done in moving a charge \(Q\) through a potential difference \(V\) is \(W = VQ\), and that energy appears as heat:

\(H = VQ = 50\,\text{V} \times 96000\,\text{C}\)

\(H = 4.8 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J}\)

The time of one hour is not needed for the heat itself — it would only be needed to work out the power.
groundedIn: §11.7 — the source supplies energy \(VQ\), and in a purely resistive circuit it is all dissipated as heat; Eq. (11.20) \(H = VIt\).

stem: An electric iron of resistance 20 \(\Omega\) takes a current of 5 A. Calculate the heat developed in 30 s.
solution:
By Joule's law of heating,

\(H = I^2 Rt\)

\(= (5\,\text{A})^2 \times 20\,\Omega \times 30\,\text{s}\)

\(= 25 \times 20 \times 30\)

\(= 15000\,\text{J} = 1.5 \times 10^{4}\,\text{J}\)
groundedIn: §11.7, Eq. (11.21) \(H = I^2 Rt\) — Joule's law of heating.

stem: What determines the rate at which energy is delivered by a current?
solution:
The rate at which energy is delivered by a current is the **electric power**, and it is determined by the potential difference across the device and the current through it:

\(P = VI = I^2 R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}\)

So for a given appliance it is fixed by the supply voltage and the appliance's own resistance.
groundedIn: §11.8, Eq. (11.22) — 'the rate of consumption of energy' is the electric power.

stem: An electric motor takes 5 A from a 220 V line. Determine the power of the motor and the energy consumed in 2 h.
solution:
Power:

\(P = VI = 220\,\text{V} \times 5\,\text{A} = 1100\,\text{W} = 1.1\,\text{kW}\)

Energy consumed in 2 hours:

\(E = P \times t = 1.1\,\text{kW} \times 2\,\text{h} = 2.2\,\text{kW h}\)

In joules, \(2.2\,\text{kW h} = 2.2 \times 3.6 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J} = 7.92 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J}\).
groundedIn: §11.8, Eq. (11.22) \(P = VI\) and the definition of the kilowatt hour, \(1\,\text{kW h} = 3.6 \times 10^6\,\text{J}\).

stem: A piece of wire of resistance \(R\) is cut into five equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel. If the equivalent resistance of this combination is \(R'\), then the ratio \(R/R'\) is –
solution:
Resistance is proportional to length, so cutting the wire into five equal parts gives five resistors of \(R/5\) each.

Five equal resistors in parallel give one fifth of the individual value:

\(R' = \dfrac{R/5}{5} = \dfrac{R}{25}\)

Therefore

\(\dfrac{R}{R'} = 25\)
groundedIn: §11.5, Eq. (11.10) for length-proportionality, and §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18) for the parallel combination.

stem: Which of the following terms does not represent electrical power in a circuit?
solution:
The three standard expressions for electric power are

\(P = VI = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}\)

So \(I^2R\), \(VI\) and \(V^2/R\) all represent power.

\(IR^2\) does not. Substituting \(V = IR\) into none of the forms produces it, and a units check settles it: \(IR^2\) has units \(\text{A}\,\Omega^2\), not watts.

stem: An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. When it is operated on 110 V, the power consumed will be –
solution:
The resistance of the bulb is fixed by its rating:

\(R = \dfrac{V^2}{P} = \dfrac{(220\,\text{V})^2}{100\,\text{W}} = 484\,\Omega\)

At 110 V the same resistance gives

\(P' = \dfrac{V'^2}{R} = \dfrac{(110\,\text{V})^2}{484\,\Omega} = \dfrac{12100}{484} = 25\,\text{W}\)

Halving the voltage quarters the power, because \(P \propto V^2\) at constant resistance. The common mistake is to halve the power to 50 W.

stem: Two conducting wires of the same material and of equal lengths and equal diameters are first connected in series and then parallel in a circuit across the same potential difference. The ratio of heat produced in series and parallel combinations would be –
solution:
The two wires are identical; let each have resistance \(R\).

In series: \(R_s = 2R\). In parallel: \(R_p = R/2\).

The potential difference \(V\) and the time \(t\) are the same in both cases, so use the form of Joule's law that holds \(V\) fixed:

\(H = \dfrac{V^2 t}{R}\)

\(\dfrac{H_s}{H_p} = \dfrac{V^2 t / R_s}{V^2 t / R_p} = \dfrac{R_p}{R_s} = \dfrac{R/2}{2R} = \dfrac{1}{4}\)

So the ratio is **1 : 4**. Note that \(H = I^2Rt\) would mislead here, because the current is *not* the same in the two arrangements — the potential difference is.
groundedIn: §11.7, Eq. (11.20)-(11.21), combined with the series and parallel rules of §11.6.1 and §11.6.2.

stem: How is a voltmeter connected in the circuit to measure the potential difference between two points?
solution:
A voltmeter is always connected **in parallel**, across the two points between which the potential difference is to be measured.

Its positive terminal goes to the point at higher potential. A voltmeter is built with a very high resistance so that it draws almost no current itself and therefore does not disturb the circuit it is measuring.
groundedIn: §11.2 — 'The voltmeter is always connected in parallel across the points between which the potential difference is to be measured.'

stem: A copper wire has diameter 0.5 mm and resistivity of \(1.6 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\). What will be the length of this wire to make its resistance 10 \(\Omega\)? How much does the resistance change if the diameter is doubled?
solution:
Radius \(r = \dfrac{0.5\,\text{mm}}{2} = 0.25\,\text{mm} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}\).

Area of cross-section:

\(A = \pi r^2 = \pi (2.5 \times 10^{-4})^2 = 1.96 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}^2\)

From \(R = \rho l / A\),

\(l = \dfrac{RA}{\rho} = \dfrac{10\,\Omega \times 1.96 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}^2}{1.6 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}} = 122.7\,\text{m}\)

**If the diameter is doubled**, the area of cross-section becomes four times as large. Since \(R \propto 1/A\) for the same length and material, the resistance becomes **one quarter** of its former value, that is \(2.5\,\Omega\).

stem:
The values of current \(I\) flowing in a given resistor for the corresponding values of potential difference \(V\) across the resistor are given below –

| \(I\) (amperes) | 0.5 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 4.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(V\) (volts) | 1.6 | 3.4 | 6.7 | 10.2 | 13.2 |

Plot a graph between \(V\) and \(I\) and calculate the resistance of that resistor.
solution:
Plot \(V\) on the vertical axis against \(I\) on the horizontal axis. The points lie very nearly on a straight line through the origin, which is what Ohm's law predicts: \(V \propto I\).

The resistance is the slope of that line, \(R = V/I\). Taking each pair in turn:

| \(I\) (A) | 0.5 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 4.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(V/I\) (\(\Omega\)) | 3.2 | 3.4 | 3.35 | 3.4 | 3.3 |

The mean value is

\(R = \dfrac{3.2 + 3.4 + 3.35 + 3.4 + 3.3}{5} = \dfrac{16.65}{5} = 3.33\,\Omega\)

So the resistance of the resistor is about \(3.3\,\Omega\). The small scatter is experimental error, not a failure of Ohm's law.
groundedIn: §11.4 Ohm's law — the \(V\)-\(I\) graph of a metallic conductor is a straight line whose slope is the resistance.

stem: When a 12 V battery is connected across an unknown resistor, there is a current of 2.5 mA in the circuit. Find the value of the resistance of the resistor.
solution:
\(V = 12\,\text{V}\), \(I = 2.5\,\text{mA} = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{A}\).

From Ohm's law,

\(R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{12\,\text{V}}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{A}} = 4800\,\Omega = 4.8\,\text{k}\Omega\)

stem: A battery of 9 V is connected in series with resistors of 0.2 \(\Omega\), 0.3 \(\Omega\), 0.4 \(\Omega\), 0.5 \(\Omega\) and 12 \(\Omega\), respectively. How much current would flow through the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor?
solution:
In a series circuit the same current flows through every resistor, so the current through the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor is just the circuit current.

Total resistance:

\(R_s = 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 + 0.5 + 12 = 13.4\,\Omega\)

Current:

\(I = \dfrac{V}{R_s} = \dfrac{9\,\text{V}}{13.4\,\Omega} = 0.67\,\text{A}\)

So about \(0.67\,\text{A}\) flows through the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor — and through every other resistor too.
groundedIn: §11.6.1, Eq. (11.14), and the statement there that the current is the same through each resistor in series.

stem: How many 176 \(\Omega\) resistors (in parallel) are required to carry 5 A on a 220 V line?
solution:
The combination must have a total resistance of

\(R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{220\,\text{V}}{5\,\text{A}} = 44\,\Omega\)

For \(n\) equal resistors of \(176\,\Omega\) in parallel,

\(R_p = \dfrac{176}{n}\)

Setting \(\dfrac{176}{n} = 44\) gives

\(n = \dfrac{176}{44} = 4\)

So **four** 176 \(\Omega\) resistors are required.
groundedIn: §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18), with Ohm's law from §11.4.

stem: Show how you would connect three resistors, each of resistance 6 \(\Omega\), so that the combination has a resistance of (i) 9 \(\Omega\), (ii) 4 \(\Omega\).
solution:
**(i) 9 \(\Omega\)** — connect two of the resistors in parallel, and the third in series with that pair.

The parallel pair:

\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{2}{6}\), so \(R_p = 3\,\Omega\)

In series with the third:

\(R = 3\,\Omega + 6\,\Omega = 9\,\Omega\)

**(ii) 4 \(\Omega\)** — connect two of the resistors in series, and the third in parallel across that pair.

The series pair:

\(R_s = 6\,\Omega + 6\,\Omega = 12\,\Omega\)

In parallel with the third:

\(\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1 + 2}{12} = \dfrac{3}{12}\), so \(R = 4\,\Omega\)
groundedIn: §11.6.1, Eq. (11.14) and §11.6.2, Eq. (11.18); Example 11.9 is the model for mixing the two rules.

stem: Several electric bulbs designed to be used on a 220 V electric supply line, are rated 10 W. How many lamps can be connected in parallel with each other across the two wires of 220 V line if the maximum allowable current is 5 A?
solution:
Current drawn by one lamp:

\(I_1 = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{10\,\text{W}}{220\,\text{V}} = \dfrac{1}{22}\,\text{A}\)

The lamps are in parallel, so the total current is the sum of the individual currents. If \(n\) lamps draw the maximum allowable 5 A,

\(n = \dfrac{5\,\text{A}}{1/22\,\text{A}} = 5 \times 22 = 110\)

So **110 lamps** can be connected.
groundedIn: §11.8, Eq. (11.22) \(P = VI\), and §11.6.2, Eq. (11.15) — the total current is the sum of the branch currents.

stem: A hot plate of an electric oven connected to a 220 V line has two resistance coils A and B, each of 24 \(\Omega\) resistance, which may be used separately, in series, or in parallel. What are the currents in the three cases?
solution:
**Separately** — one coil of 24 \(\Omega\) across 220 V:

\(I = \dfrac{220}{24} = 9.2\,\text{A}\)

**In series** — \(R_s = 24 + 24 = 48\,\Omega\):

\(I = \dfrac{220}{48} = 4.6\,\text{A}\)

**In parallel** — \(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{24} = \dfrac{2}{24}\), so \(R_p = 12\,\Omega\):

\(I = \dfrac{220}{12} = 18.3\,\text{A}\)

The parallel arrangement draws the largest current and so gives the hottest setting.

stem: Compare the power used in the 2 \(\Omega\) resistor in each of the following circuits: (i) a 6 V battery in series with 1 \(\Omega\) and 2 \(\Omega\) resistors, and (ii) a 4 V battery in parallel with 12 \(\Omega\) and 2 \(\Omega\) resistors.
solution:
**(i) Series, 6 V with 1 \(\Omega\) and 2 \(\Omega\).**

Total resistance \(= 1 + 2 = 3\,\Omega\), so the current is

\(I = \dfrac{6\,\text{V}}{3\,\Omega} = 2\,\text{A}\)

The same current passes through the 2 \(\Omega\) resistor, so

\(P = I^2 R = (2)^2 \times 2 = 8\,\text{W}\)

**(ii) Parallel, 4 V across 12 \(\Omega\) and 2 \(\Omega\).**

In a parallel combination each branch has the full supply voltage across it, so the 2 \(\Omega\) resistor has 4 V across it:

\(P = \dfrac{V^2}{R} = \dfrac{(4)^2}{2} = 8\,\text{W}\)

**The power used in the 2 \(\Omega\) resistor is 8 W in both circuits** — they are equal. Note that the 12 \(\Omega\) resistor in (ii) makes no difference to the 2 \(\Omega\) branch at all.
groundedIn: §11.8, Eq. (11.22), with the series and parallel current/voltage rules of §11.6.1 and §11.6.2.

stem: Two lamps, one rated 100 W at 220 V, and the other 60 W at 220 V, are connected in parallel to electric mains supply. What current is drawn from the line if the supply voltage is 220 V?
solution:
Both lamps are operated at their rated voltage, so each consumes its rated power. In parallel the powers add:

\(P = 100\,\text{W} + 60\,\text{W} = 160\,\text{W}\)

Current drawn from the line:

\(I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{160\,\text{W}}{220\,\text{V}} = 0.73\,\text{A}\)
groundedIn: §11.8, Eq. (11.22) \(P = VI\), and §11.6.2 — each parallel branch has the full supply voltage across it.

stem: Which uses more energy, a 250 W TV set in 1 hr, or a 1200 W toaster in 10 minutes?
solution:
Energy is power multiplied by time.

TV set:

\(E = 250\,\text{W} \times 1\,\text{h} = 250\,\text{W h}\)

Toaster:

\(E = 1200\,\text{W} \times \dfrac{10}{60}\,\text{h} = 200\,\text{W h}\)

So the **250 W TV set in 1 hour** uses more energy — 250 W h against 200 W h. The toaster draws far more power, but for only a sixth of the time.
groundedIn: §11.8 — energy is the product of power and time, measured in watt hours.

stem: An electric heater of resistance 44 \(\Omega\) draws 5 A from the service mains for 2 hours. Calculate the rate at which heat is developed in the heater.
solution:
The *rate* at which heat is developed is the power:

\(P = I^2 R = (5\,\text{A})^2 \times 44\,\Omega = 25 \times 44 = 1100\,\text{W}\)

So heat is developed at \(1100\,\text{J}\) per second.

The 2 hours in the question is not needed for the *rate* — it would only be needed to find the total heat, which would be \(1100\,\text{W} \times 7200\,\text{s} = 7.92 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J}\).
groundedIn: §11.7, Eq. (11.21) \(H = I^2Rt\), so the rate of heating is \(I^2R\).

stem: Why is the tungsten used almost exclusively for filament of electric lamps?
solution:
A lamp filament has to be made white-hot without melting, so it needs a metal with a **very high melting point** — tungsten melts at 3380°C.

Tungsten also has a **high resistivity** \(\left(5.20 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\right)\) so that a great deal of heat is produced in it, and it **retains that heat** rather than losing it, so it gets hot enough to emit light.
groundedIn: §11.7.1 — 'A strong metal with high melting point such as tungsten (melting point 3380°C) is used for making bulb filaments'; the resistivity figure is from Table 11.2.

stem: Why are the conductors of electric heating devices, such as bread-toasters and electric irons, made of an alloy rather than a pure metal?
solution:
Because an alloy has a **higher resistivity** than its constituent pure metals, so for the same current it produces much more heat \(\left(H = I^2Rt\right)\).

Also, **alloys do not oxidise or burn readily at high temperatures**, so the heating element lasts instead of corroding away each time it is run red-hot.
groundedIn: §11.5 — 'the resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals. Alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures.'

stem: Why is the series arrangement not used for domestic circuits?
solution:
Several reasons, all of which follow from how a series circuit behaves:

- **One failure stops everything.** If any one appliance fails the circuit is broken and none of the others works.
- **Every appliance is forced to carry the same current.** Domestic appliances need very different currents — a bulb and a heater cannot sensibly share one.
- **The supply voltage is divided** among the appliances, so none of them receives the full 220 V it is rated for.
- Appliances **cannot be switched on and off independently**.
groundedIn: §11.6.2 — the discussion after Example 11.9 on why series circuits are impracticable, including the fairy-lights example.

stem: How does the resistance of a wire vary with its area of cross-section?
solution:
The resistance of a wire is **inversely proportional** to its area of cross-section:

\(R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}\)

So for a given material and length, doubling the area halves the resistance. A thick wire therefore offers less resistance than a thin one.

stem: Why are copper and aluminium wires usually employed for electricity transmission?
solution:
Because copper and aluminium have **very low resistivity** — \(1.62 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\) and \(2.63 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\) respectively, among the lowest of any material in Table 11.2.

Low resistivity means low resistance in a long transmission line, so very little of the transmitted energy is wasted as heat \(\left(H = I^2Rt\right)\) on the way. They are also ductile enough to be drawn into long wires and cheap enough to use in quantity.
groundedIn: §11.5 — 'copper and aluminium are generally used for electrical transmission lines'; the resistivity figures are from Table 11.2.
